content:
Most Indian NGOs that fundraise online end up using both: a crowdfunding platform for reach and quick campaigns, and their own website as the permanent home where donors can verify who they are, give directly and hear from them again. If you must choose one to build first, the deciding questions are who owns the donor relationship, what each rupee raised actually costs after all fees, whether you can issue compliant receipts and handle foreign donations, and how much effort you can put into driving traffic yourself. This guide is for founders, trustees and fundraising managers of registered NGOs comparing NGO website development in India with simply starting a campaign on a crowdfunding platform. It does not recommend any particular platform and does not quote platform fees, because those change and differ by plan; it shows you how to ask the right questions and compare on equal terms.

You will find here what a crowdfunding page does well, what an owned donation website does well, a side-by-side comparison, the legal and compliance points to check before either, a worked cost model with clearly labelled assumed numbers, a hybrid approach that most mid-sized NGOs end up adopting, and a short list of questions to put to any platform in writing before you sign up.

## The two models in plain terms

A **crowdfunding or donation platform** is a third-party website where you create a campaign page, share it, and donors pay through the platform. The platform handles the page, the payment processing and usually the first-level communication with donors. It earns through fees, tips from donors or both, depending on its model.

An **owned donation website** is your NGO's own site with a donation page connected to a payment gateway that you hold an account with. You control the design, the data, the receipts and the donor communication. You are also responsible for hosting, security, maintenance and for bringing visitors to the site.

Neither is automatically better. They solve different problems.

## What crowdfunding platforms do well

- **A fast start.** A campaign page can be live within days, with no development work. For an urgent medical appeal, a disaster response or a small first campaign, that speed matters.
- **Built-in payments and tools.** Payment collection, basic updates and sharing buttons are included.
- **A familiar interface for donors.** Some donors have given through a platform before and are comfortable doing so again.
- **Possible discovery.** Some platforms surface campaigns to their own audience. How much that helps varies widely by cause and platform, and you should not plan around discovery you cannot verify.
- **Lower upfront cost.** You pay as you raise rather than building something first.

## What crowdfunding platforms do not do well for an organisation

- **Donor relationship.** On many platforms, you receive limited donor details, or receive them subject to the platform's terms and the donor's choices. If you cannot contact donors again, each campaign starts from zero. Check what contact details you receive, whether donors have consented to hear from you, and for how long you can use them.
- **Brand and trust.** The page sits on someone else's domain with someone else's branding around it. Donors who want to verify an NGO often look for its own website, registration numbers and annual reports.
- **Compliance fit.** Receipts, tax-benefit documentation and foreign donation rules depend on the platform's arrangement with you. Some arrangements work well; others place burdens on you. See the compliance section below.
- **Fee layers.** There can be a platform fee, a payment processing fee, taxes on those fees and sometimes a donor tip. The headline number is rarely the whole picture.
- **Dependency.** The platform can change its fees, policies or search ranking, or suspend a campaign, and you have little recourse.
- **Search visibility.** A campaign page on a platform may rank for your campaign title, but your organisation does not build up its own search presence from it. Our guide to [SEO page planning for NGO websites](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-seo-page-planning-donors-2026) shows what an owned site can build over time.

## What an owned donation website does well

- **You own the relationship.** With a proper consent process, donor details go into your own system. You can thank, update and invite them again, which is where most of the long-term value of fundraising sits. See [donor CRM software for Indian NGOs](/blog/ngo-donor-crm-software-india-2026).
- **Credibility.** A site showing your registration details, trustees, programmes, reports and contact information answers the first questions a cautious donor asks. Our articles on the [About and governance page](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-about-governance-page-trustees-team-policies-2026) and the [contact and grievance page](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-contact-grievance-page-trust-safeguarding-2026) describe what to publish.
- **Flexible giving options.** One-time, monthly, in memory of someone, festival campaigns, event registrations and peer-to-peer pages can all be designed to fit your programme. See [recurring monthly giving](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-recurring-monthly-giving-2026) and [peer-to-peer fundraising pages](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-peer-to-peer-fundraising-pages-2026).
- **Receipts and records on your terms.** Receipts can carry the details your auditors and donors need, and be generated automatically.
- **Lower marginal fees at scale.** There is no platform fee on top of the payment gateway's charges, though you carry the cost of building and running the site.
- **A base for everything else.** Email, WhatsApp, search and social all point somewhere. An owned site is the place they should point.

## What an owned site demands from you

- **Build and maintenance cost.** See our [NGO website cost guide](/blog/ngo-website-cost-india-complete-guide) for ranges and what drives them.
- **Traffic.** A new donation page has no audience. Visitors must come from your email list, social channels, events, search and partners.
- **Payment setup.** You need a payment gateway account approved for non-profit use, which involves documentation and sometimes waiting time.
- **Security and uptime.** Donation pages are a target for card-testing bots and other abuse; see [donation site security and hosting](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-donation-site-security-hosting-2026).
- **Someone to run it.** Updating campaigns, responding to donor queries and reconciling payments need a named person.

## Side-by-side comparison

| Question | Crowdfunding platform | Owned donation website |
|---|---|---|
| How quickly can you start? | Days | Weeks, depending on scope |
| Who holds the donor data? | Depends on the platform's terms | You, if set up with consent |
| Who controls the brand and message? | Shared with the platform's design | You |
| Fee structure | Platform fee, payment fee, possible tip, taxes on fees (check each) | Payment gateway fee plus your own build and running cost |
| Receipts and tax documents | Varies; verify who issues them | Issued by you with your details |
| Foreign contributions | Check carefully; see below | Possible only with the right registration and bank arrangement |
| Discovery of new donors | Possible, unpredictable | Only through your own promotion |
| Long-term search presence | Limited to the campaign page | Builds over time |
| Risk of policy change or suspension | Higher | Lower, though your gateway has rules too |
| Effort to run | Low | Medium |

## Compliance points to check before choosing

This section is general information, not legal or tax advice. Rules change; confirm with a chartered accountant or an advocate who works with NGOs.

### Tax-deductible donations and receipts

If your NGO has a valid registration under the Income-tax Act that allows donors to claim a deduction under section 80G, donors will want a receipt that meets the requirements, and the NGO has reporting duties for donations eligible for that benefit. Our articles on [12A and 80G renewal](/blog/12a-80g-renewal-checklist-ngos) and the [12A registration process](/blog/12a-registration-ngos-documents-process) explain the registrations. When you use a platform, find out in writing: who issues the receipt, in whose name, whether it carries your registration details, whether it is issued automatically, and how donor PAN or address details required for the receipt are collected and passed to you. If the platform's receipt is only a payment acknowledgement, you may need to issue your own.

### Foreign donations

Receiving foreign contribution in India is governed by the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act and its rules. An NGO needs the appropriate FCRA registration or prior permission and must receive such funds through the designated bank account. Many domestic crowdfunding pages are set up for rupee donations from Indian residents; accepting foreign cards or foreign donors on a page is a separate question that depends on your FCRA status and the platform's arrangement. Do not assume that because a donor can pay from abroad, you are permitted to accept it. Read our article on the [FCRA amendment rules and your website](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-fcra-amendment-rules-2026) and ask your advisor before enabling foreign payments on any page.

### Data protection

Donor names, phone numbers, email addresses, PAN and payment details are personal data. India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 sets duties on those who decide how such data is processed. Whether you are on a platform or your own site, work out who is responsible for what, what the donor was told, and how a donor can withdraw consent. Our [DPDP checklist for NGO donation portals](/blog/checklist-for-pdp-bill-compliance-on-ngo-donation-portal-india-2026-2026) is a place to start.

### Transparency expectations

Whatever channel you use, donors increasingly expect to see where the money goes. Platforms often require updates and withdrawals to follow their rules, which can help or hinder. On your own site, you decide how to report; see our guide to [transparency and impact reporting](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-transparency-impact-reporting-2026).

## A worked cost model, with assumptions marked

The numbers below are assumed round figures to show how the arithmetic works. They are not the fees of any platform and not a benchmark. Replace them with the real figures from the written terms you are offered.

Assume a campaign collects ₹10,00,000 in one-time donations. We will compare the money your NGO receives under two assumed fee structures.

**Scenario A: platform.** Assume the platform and payment processing together take 6% of the total, and that GST on the platform's fee takes a further 1% of the total. Deductions: ₹60,000 plus ₹10,000, so the NGO receives ₹9,30,000. If donors are shown an optional tip and some leave it, that tip comes from the donor on top and is not part of this comparison, but you should know whether the page encourages it.

**Scenario B: own website.** Assume the payment gateway charges 2.5% including taxes, so ₹25,000 is deducted. The NGO receives ₹9,75,000 from the gateway. Now add the cost of the site. Suppose, again as an assumption, that the first-year cost of building and running the site is ₹1,00,000. If the site raises ₹10,00,000 in that year, the net is ₹8,75,000, lower than Scenario A for that single year. If the site raises ₹30,00,000 over the year, the gateway fee is ₹75,000 and the net after the same site cost is ₹28,25,000, against ₹27,90,000 for the platform scenario at the same assumed rate.

What the illustration shows is that fixed costs matter at low volumes and marginal fees matter at high volumes. It also leaves out the things the arithmetic cannot capture: the value of owning donor contacts, the cost of the traffic you must generate yourself, and the chance that a platform brings donors you would not have reached. A fair comparison should add your own estimate of repeat giving. If owning the relationship leads even a modest share of one-time donors to give again, the long-term math changes. We have deliberately not put a percentage on that, because it varies by cause and by how well an NGO follows up.

### A simple method for your own comparison

1. Write down the expected amount to be raised in the next twelve months through each channel.
2. List every fee in writing: platform fee, payment fee, taxes on those fees, withdrawal charges, donor tip handling, setup fee.
3. Add fixed costs: building, hosting, maintenance, the staff time to run it.
4. Estimate how many donors you could contact again and what repeat giving you might realistically expect, and mark it as an estimate.
5. Compare net amounts under a low, medium and high fundraising scenario rather than one.

## The hybrid approach most NGOs end up with

For most registered NGOs with a continuing programme, a hybrid works best.

1. **Make your own website the home base.** It holds your registration details, programmes, reports, a clear donation page and a monthly giving option.
2. **Use a crowdfunding page for specific time-bound campaigns,** such as an emergency appeal or a challenge where the platform's reach or tools genuinely help. Link the campaign page back to your website and describe the NGO properly on it.
3. **Bring donors home.** After a campaign, invite those donors, where the platform's terms allow, to join your updates on your own channels. Never scrape or misuse contact details beyond what the platform and donors permitted.
4. **Keep the records in one place.** Reconcile donations from every source into one donor list, so that a person who gave on a platform and on your site appears once.
5. **Review each year.** Compare what each channel actually delivered net of fees and effort, and shift effort accordingly.

Our article on [NGO donation page design](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-donation-page-design-2026) covers how to make the owned page convert, and [donation analytics with GA4](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-donation-analytics-ga4-funnel-2026) shows how to measure it honestly.

## Which route fits which kind of organisation

| Situation | Suggested starting point |
|---|---|
| New NGO, small team, first fundraiser, no website yet | A simple owned page or a platform campaign, while planning the site; do not wait for a perfect site to begin |
| Urgent, one-off cause appeal | Platform campaign for speed, with a short note and link to your site |
| Established NGO with regular donors and programmes | Owned website as the base, platform used selectively |
| NGO that receives CSR funding or institutional grants | Owned website with governance and reporting pages; see [CSR volunteer portals](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-csr-volunteer-portals-2026) |
| NGO that wants monthly donors | Owned website, because recurring giving depends on owning the relationship and the mandate setup |
| NGO seeking foreign donors | Owned website after confirming FCRA status; platforms only if their arrangement is clearly lawful for you |
| Individuals raising money for a person or cause without a registered organisation | Different rules and risks apply; this guide is for registered organisations |

## Questions to put to any platform in writing

1. What are all the fees, including taxes on fees, withdrawal charges and any charge for receipts?
2. What do I receive about each donor, and what may I do with it?
3. Who issues the donation receipt, and does it show my registration details?
4. How long until funds reach my account, and under what conditions can they be held?
5. Can I accept foreign donations, and what documents do you need from me?
6. What happens to my campaign page and data if I leave or you suspend my account?
7. What are the rules on campaign updates and fund use, and what happens if I breach them?
8. Does the platform add anything that I cannot control, such as ads, suggested tips or a default tip setting?

If an answer is vague, ask for it in the written terms. Keep a copy.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Treating a campaign page as a substitute for a website.
- Comparing fees using only the headline percentage.
- Forgetting taxes on platform fees.
- Letting donor details live only on someone else's dashboard.
- Accepting foreign donations on a channel without confirming FCRA compliance.
- Starting a website with no plan for how donors will find it.
- Building a site so elaborate that the team cannot maintain it.
- Failing to link the campaign page and the website to each other, which wastes the trust each could lend the other.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is it cheaper for an NGO to use a crowdfunding platform or its own website?
It depends on volume. A platform has no build cost but takes fees on each rupee raised; an owned site has build and running costs but typically lower per-donation fees. Compare using real written fee terms, your expected annual fundraising and the value of owning donor contacts.

### Can an NGO collect donations on its own website without a crowdfunding platform?
Yes. You need a payment gateway account that accepts non-profit use, a donation page that follows consent and receipt requirements, and the correct registrations for any tax-benefit or foreign-contribution claims. The details depend on your legal form and registrations.

### Who gets the donor's details on a crowdfunding platform?
It depends on the platform and its terms. Some share limited details with the campaign owner, some share more if the donor agrees. Read the terms and ask in writing what you may receive and how you may use it.

### Can I issue 80G receipts if donations come through a crowdfunding platform?
Only if your NGO holds the relevant approval and the receipt meets the requirements. Find out whether the platform issues receipts on your behalf and with your details, or whether you must issue them yourself. A chartered accountant can confirm the correct approach.

### Should a small NGO build a website first or start with a campaign?
If you have an urgent need, start with a campaign and publish a simple page about your organisation at the same time. If you are planning ongoing fundraising, build the website in parallel, because it becomes the place where donors verify you and where you keep the relationship.

## Where to Start

Take last year's donation records, or your best estimate, and list how each donor reached you. Then note which donors you can contact today. That list shows how much of your fundraising relationship you already own, and it tells you whether the next rupee of effort belongs on a campaign or on your own website.
